BibleReferences: Genesis 1:25; Genesis 1:31; Genesis 2:19; Genesis 9:9-10; Proverbs 12:10; Isaiah 11:6; Matthew 10:29; Romans 8:21-22; 1 Corinthians 15:26; Revelation 21:4; Ecclesiastes 3:19-21
DetailedAnswer:
Scripture does not explicitly tell us whether our individual pets will be resurrected, so we should not claim certainty where God has not given it. But there are strong biblical reasons to hope that animals will share in God's restoration of creation.

God created animals and declared His creation good (Genesis 1:25, 1:31). They were present in Eden before the Fall — Adam even named them (Genesis 2:19) — and they suffer under a Fall they did not cause. If animals share in creation's brokenness, why would they not share in its deliverance? Romans 8:21-22 says the whole creation groans and 'shall be delivered from the bondage of corruption into the glorious liberty of the children of God.'

God preserved animals alongside humanity in the Flood and included living creatures in His covenant with Noah (Genesis 9:9-10). He commands us to treat them with care — 'A righteous man regardeth the life of his beast' (Proverbs 12:10) — and Jesus says not even a sparrow falls without our Father (Matthew 10:29).

Scripture's visions of restored peace are described with animals: 'The wolf also shall dwell with the lamb' (Isaiah 11:6), and 'there shall be no more death' (Revelation 21:4). Death is 'the last enemy that shall be destroyed' (1 Corinthians 15:26). Humans alone are made in God's image, and Ecclesiastes 3:19-21 honestly leaves the destiny of beasts an open question — animals are distinct from us, but distinct does not mean forgotten.

The absence of an explicit promise is not an explicit denial. We cannot guarantee we will be reunited with every beloved pet, but the pattern of Scripture — a good creation, a shared Fall, a promised restoration of all creation — gives us real reason to hope their suffering and death are not the end of their story.

Read the full biblical case in the blog post 'Do Animals Go to Heaven? A Biblical Case for Hope in God's Redemption of Creation.'
